# Lab 1 — Deploy OWASP Juice Shop and Set Up the Course Workflow

## Task 1 — Deploy Juice Shop and write a triage report

### Asset

- **Image tag:** `bkimminich/juice-shop:v20.0.0`
- **Image digest:** `bkimminich/juice-shop@sha256:fd58bdc9745416afce8184ee0666278a436574633ea7880365153a63bfd418b0`
- **Host OS:** Ubuntu 25.10
- **Docker version:** Docker version 29.1.3, build `29.1.3-0ubuntu3~25.10.1`

The image digest identifies the exact immutable image content used in this run,
while the tag is the human-readable version reference.

<img alt="Task 1 asset host OS evidence" src="data:image/png;base64," />

### Deployment

The container was started with:

```bash
docker run -d --name juice-shop -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop:v20.0.0
```

The application was available at `http://127.0.0.1:3000`. The mapping
`127.0.0.1:3000->3000/tcp` binds the published port to the host loopback
interface, so other hosts cannot connect to this deliberately vulnerable
application directly through the network. The observed restart policy was
`no`, meaning Docker will not automatically restart the container after it
stops.

<img alt="Task 1 restart-policy evidence" src="data:image/png;base64," />

### Health

The health checks produced the following observed results:

- `docker ps`: `juice-shop   Up About a minute   127.0.0.1:3000->3000/tcp`
- Request to `/`: `HTTP 200`
- Application version: `{"version":"20.0.0"}`
- Product count: `46`

Together, these checks show that the container was running, the root route
responded successfully, the expected application version was deployed, and the
product data path returned the expected number of records. The product count
does not independently prove that a live database query occurred because the
response could also come from cached or preloaded data.

The following capture records the container, health, version, product-count,
image-digest, and Docker-version checks.

<img alt="Task 1.1 terminal evidence for the Juice Shop deployment and health checks" src="data:image/png;base64," />

### Surface

- **Login and registration:** The **Account** menu exposed the login page, which
  contained email and password fields, password recovery, a **Remember me**
  option, and a link for new customers to reach registration.
- **Products:** The product list loaded on the home page. Opening a product
  generated requests for product data and reviews without requiring
  authentication.
- **Admin or account area:** Selecting **Account** while unauthenticated
  redirected to `/#/login`. No administrative area was visible to an
  unauthenticated user.
- **Console errors:** Initially, no console errors were observed. Later, the
  login page Console showed a request to `/rest/user/login` returning `401
  Unauthorized`. Directly opening that unexpected path produced an HTTP `500`
  response with an Express stack trace, and Juice Shop then displayed a
  notification that the **Error Handling** challenge had been solved.

<img alt="Juice Shop HTTP 500 response exposing the Express version, internal paths, source locations, and stack trace for the unexpected /rest/user/login path" src="data:image/png;base64," />

<img alt="Juice Shop Error Handling challenge notification with the DevTools Console showing an HTTP 401 Unauthorized login request" src="data:image/png;base64," />
- **Browser storage:** Before authentication, Local Storage was empty. The
  application had two cookies: `language=en`, which stores the language
  preference, and `cookieconsent_status=dismiss`, which records the cookie
  banner choice. No authentication or session token was present.

<img alt="Juice Shop Local Storage view showing no stored keys before authentication" src="data:image/png;base64," />

<img alt="Juice Shop cookies showing language and cookie consent preferences" src="data:image/png;base64," />


### Headers

Command:

```bash
curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:3000 | head -20
```

Observed output:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Feature-Policy: payment 'self'
X-Recruiting: /#/jobs
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0
Last-Modified: Mon, 28 Sep 2026 12:16:02 GMT
ETag: W/"26af-1a0e7f18f35"
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 9903
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Date: Mon, 28 Sep 2026 12:43:11 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
```

- **`Content-Security-Policy`: missing.** Without a CSP, the browser has no application-defined allowlist restricting where scripts and other resources may load from. This removes a defense-in-depth control that can limit the impact of injected content, although the missing header alone does not prove that JavaScript injection is possible.
- **`Strict-Transport-Security`: missing.** The browser is not instructed to force future connections to use HTTPS. This does not prevent HTTPS from being used; it means HTTPS is not enforced through HSTS. The application was accessed over plain HTTP in this local lab.
- **`X-Content-Type-Options`: present as `nosniff`.** The browser is instructed to honor declared content types instead of MIME-sniffing a response as another executable type.
- **`X-Frame-Options`: present as `SAMEORIGIN`.** The page may be framed only by a page from the same origin, reducing exposure to cross-origin clickjacking.

The two missing headers represent absent security hardening and are classified as **OWASP Top 10:2025 A02 — Security Misconfiguration**.

<img alt="HTTP response headers showing X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options present while CSP and HSTS are absent" src="data:image/png;base64," />

### Top 3 risks

1. **Missing Content Security Policy — A02: Security Misconfiguration.**
   The application did not provide a Content Security Policy, removing a
   browser-enforced restriction on which scripts and resources may execute. If
   another vulnerability allowed malicious content to be injected, the missing
   CSP could increase its impact by leaving the browser with one fewer layer to
   block the injected script; its absence alone does not prove that an XSS
   vulnerability exists.

2. **Unencrypted and unenforced transport — A04: Cryptographic Failures.**
   The application was served over plain HTTP, and the response did not include
   HSTS to enforce future HTTPS connections. If this configuration were exposed
   over a network, an attacker able to intercept the traffic could read or
   modify transmitted data, including credentials or session information; the
   localhost-only binding limits this exposure in the current lab.

3. **Inconsistent and revealing error handling — A10: Mishandling of
   Exceptional Conditions.** An unexpected request returned HTTP `500` and
   exposed the Express version, internal paths, source locations, and a stack
   trace. These implementation details can help an attacker understand the
   application and refine later attacks, while the successful Error Handling
   challenge confirms that the failure was not handled gracefully or
   consistently.

## Task 2 — PR template

The pull request template was created at `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`.
It defines the required sections:

- `Goal`
- `Changes`
- `Testing`
- `Artifacts & Screenshots`

The template also includes the required checklist items:

- `The title follows feat(labN): <topic>.`
- `No secrets or large temporary files are committed.`
- `submissions/labN.md exists.`

Draft PR: <https://github.com/inno-devops-labs/DevSecOps-Intro/pull/1799>

The auto-fill behavior was validated by opening a PR form in the fork after the
template had been added to the fork's `main` branch. The description box loaded
the template sections and checklist before any manual PR description content was
entered.

<img alt="Task 2 pull request template auto-fill evidence" src="data:image/png;base64," />

## Task 3 — GitHub community

Foram adicionadas estrelas ao repositório do curso e ao projeto Simple Container API,
e foram seguidos o professor e cinco colegas. As estrelas ajudam mantenedores de
projetos open source porque sinalizam interesse e adoção, aumentam a visibilidade do
projeto e ajudam outras pessoas a encontrá-lo. Seguir participantes de uma equipe
facilita acompanhar suas atividades públicas, descobrir os repositórios em que
trabalham e manter contato com o trabalho desenvolvido em conjunto.

## Bonus: CI smoke test

The smoke test workflow was added at `.github/workflows/lab1-smoke.yml`.
It runs on `pull_request` events targeting `main`, uses workflow-level
`permissions: contents: read`, starts `bkimminich/juice-shop:v20.0.0` as a
service container, and polls `http://localhost:3000/rest/admin/application-version`
with `curl --silent --fail` for up to 60 seconds.

Run URL: <https://github.com/rmcavalcante7/DevSecOps-Intro/actions/runs/36532579603>

The successful job ran from `2026-09-29T06:43:37Z` to
`2026-09-29T06:43:56Z`, for a duration of approximately 19 seconds. The full
workflow run completed successfully at `2026-09-29T06:43:57Z`.

Curl output excerpt:

```text
Waiting for Juice Shop (1/12)...
{"version":"20.0.0"}Juice Shop is ready on attempt 2.
```

The same workflow was also attached to the official course draft PR, but GitHub
marked that run as `action_required` before creating any jobs because the course
repository requires approval before running Actions from forked pull requests.
